_about: Zoning cells (PRD, "M2 Zoning and buildings"). Every zonable segment gets square cells along both sides, reaching back from the road's edge. `maxSlope` is the steepest ground, rise over run at a cell's centre, that a cell can be zoned on. It is a starting value to tune, a little steeper than the steepest street (0.16), since a building can step down ground a road cannot climb. `settleCellsPerTick` is how many cells a change of roads may walk in one tick; a bigger change settles over the next few ticks, and the tick it is done by is part of the city's state (cell-index.ts). Set so a slice takes about a quarter of the 20 ms tick budget on a CI runner, which leaves room for a garbage collection landing in the same step; at 6,000 a slice took 8 to 11 ms and one with a collection in it went over. A cell that changes sends the cells after it round again, so a walk can take more than its counted size: `settleRewalkAllowance` is what the size is multiplied by when the ready tick is chosen, so the step before that tick, which walks whatever is left, is not left a pile. Measured on the soak city, walks took up to 17% more than their size. Finding the cells a change reaches counts against it too: `settleSurfacePieceCost` for each piece of road surface that comes or goes, and `settleFiledCellCost` for each cell filed in or out of the index, both in cells walked, measured on the 30,000 segment city. `maxRectsPerCommand` is the most rectangles one `ZoneCells` may carry, and `maxRectSide` the longest side, in metres, any of them may have; together they keep the step that applies one inside the tick budget (zone.ts). Starting values to tune. `throughLotMaxGap` is the widest gap, in metres, a through-lot (M2-14) may leave between the backs of the two strips it joins, measured corner to corner, so it also bounds how far the two strips' cells may be out of line along the road: a block drawn by hand a little deeper than two strips leaves a sliver, and half a cell is the starting value to tune. No prices here, so no source years.
